readerTitle: Your power in a deal comes from what you'd do without it
caseNote: 실제 연구 개념 (Fisher & Ury, Getting to Yes) + 가상 사례 (청소 업체, 번역 회사)
insight: 협상력은 테이블 위의 논리가 아니라 테이블 밖에 준비해 둔 대안에서 나온다.
misconception: 좋은 자료와 설득력 있는 논리를 준비하면 협상에서 이긴다. 큰 쪽이 항상 유리하다.

sources.text: Fisher, R. & Ury, W. (1981). Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In. Houghton Mifflin.
청소 업체와 번역 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: BATNA(Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement)라는 용어가 Fisher & Ury의 1981년 'Getting to Yes'에서 소개되었다는 점을 게시 전 재확인하세요.
5번 카드의 3단계(대안 나열 → 유망한 대안 구체화 → 최선 선택)는 Getting to Yes의 BATNA 개발 절차를 요약한 것입니다. 원문 표현과 일치하는지 확인하세요.
청소 업체의 매출 비중 60%, 15% 인하 요구 등은 모두 가상 수치이며 계산이 필요한 부분은 없습니다.

cards.title: The better pitch lost.
body: Maya runs a 12-person office cleaning company. One property manager brings in 60% of her revenue. At renewal, they ask for a 15% price cut.
She spends a week on the perfect case: inspection scores, staff training records, zero complaints in two years. It's the strongest argument in the room. It doesn't matter.

image.label: A polished presentation on a table, a phone with no contacts beside it
image.brief: 회의 테이블 위에 잘 만든 프레젠테이션 자료(그래프, 체크 표시)가 펼쳐져 있고, 그 옆에 연락처가 텅 빈 휴대폰. 따뜻한 톤의 일러스트. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You have one week before the meeting.
body: You're Maya. The client wants 15% off. You can only do one thing well this week.
Where do you spend the time?

options.text: Build a sharp deck showing your quality and track record
options.feedback: A good case helps the client justify paying you. But if they don't believe you'd ever leave, they can admire the deck and still insist on the cut.

options.text: Work out what you'd actually do if this client left, and start making it real
options.feedback: Calling prospects and pricing out a plan B costs you the polished deck. It gives you something stronger: the ability to say no and mean it.

options.text: Offer a 5% cut up front to show goodwill
options.feedback: It may set a friendly tone, but you give away money before learning anything. And it signals you're worried about losing them.

cards.title: Same request, two different answers.
body: In the meeting, the client said another firm had quoted lower. Maya had no other large client and no plan if this one walked. Everyone at the table could sense it. She accepted the 15% cut.

Across town, a rival cleaner got the same request from the same client. Her business was spread across four mid-sized clients, and she had two prospects asking for quotes. She calmly said no. **The client kept her at full price.**

cards.title: Your best alternative
body: Negotiation researchers Roger Fisher and William Ury named this idea in their 1981 book *Getting to Yes*: your **BATNA**, or Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement.
It's simply what you will do if this deal doesn't happen. Not the outcome you hope for. The real plan you'd carry out tomorrow.
The better your alternative, the less you need this particular deal. That, more than any argument, is where bargaining power comes from.

image.label: Two paths from a negotiating table: deal or plan B
image.brief: 협상 테이블에서 두 갈래 길이 나뉘는 그림. 한쪽은 "This deal", 다른 쪽은 "Your best alternative". 대안 쪽 길이 탄탄하고 밝게 표현되어 있음. 로고 없음.

cards.title: An alternative is built, not found.
body: Fisher and Ury suggest three steps before any important negotiation:
list: **List** everything you could do if talks fail: other clients, other suppliers, doing it yourself, waiting
**Develop** the most promising ones into real options: make calls, get quotes, check numbers
**Pick** the single best one. That's your BATNA
cards.callout: Maya's week was better spent on step two than on slides.
cards.softwareNote: For a software company selling to one big customer, a BATNA looks like a healthy sales pipeline. A founder with three serious prospects negotiates a large contract very differently from one with none.

cards.title: The client has a best alternative too.
body: "Another firm quoted lower" sounds strong. But switching cleaners isn't free for the client. A new crew needs keys, security checks and time to learn each building. Tenants complain while they do.
So the client's real alternative is cheaper invoices plus months of hassle. Maya treated it as a sure thing. It wasn't.
Estimating their alternative is as important as knowing your own. Often it's weaker than they make it sound.

image.label: Scale weighing a lower quote against switching hassles
image.brief: 저울 그림. 한쪽에 "Lower quote" 가격표, 다른 쪽에 열쇠 꾸러미, 보안 점검표, 불만 쪽지 같은 "전환 비용" 아이템들이 쌓여 있음. 로고 없음.

cards.title: A pretend alternative is worse than none.
body: Your BATNA only works if it's real. Bluffing about other offers can collapse the moment someone asks for details, and it damages trust you'll need later.
A strong alternative also isn't a threat to wave around. Usually it just lets you stay calm and say no to bad terms.
And knowing your alternative doesn't yet tell you your exact limit. Turning it into a number is the next step.

cards.title: Now it's a translation agency.
body: You run a B2B translation agency. Your biggest client, a medical device maker, says it will switch to a machine translation tool unless you cut rates by 25%.
What's your first move?

options.text: Agree to a smaller cut right away so they don't leave
options.feedback: It may keep the client, but you lower your price based on a threat you haven't tested. They'll likely ask again next year.

options.text: Check your own pipeline, and ask what switching would really cost them
options.feedback: It takes time before answering. But medical documents still need expert review and regulatory sign-off, so their alternative may be weaker than it sounds, and you'll know how much you need them.

options.text: Tell them you have other big clients lined up, even though you don't
options.feedback: It might buy a moment of leverage. If they call your bluff, you've lost both the price and your credibility.

cards.title: Prepare your alternative before you prepare your argument.
body: In any deal, your strength comes from what you'd do without it. Build that plan first, then estimate theirs.
**Try it today:** pick your most important customer or supplier. Write one sentence: "If they left tomorrow, I would…" If you can't finish it, that's your project this month.
